source.title: Mitigating multiple descents: A model-agnostic framework for risk monotonization
source.authors: Pratik V. Patil; A. Kuchibhotla; Yuting Wei; A. Rinaldo

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some mathematical notation is corrupted by text conversion, but the relevant prose, equations, and figure descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports risk profiles and simulations for linear prediction procedures across feature-to-sample ratios, bearing on double descent in those settings, but does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's own baseline MN2LS and MN1LS risk profiles and its comparison of optimally tuned ridge and lasso bear on the claim. Results for the proposed zero-step and one-step procedures are not rows: they concern deliberately modified procedures, not whether the base procedures exhibit double descent. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as results. The study does not sweep training epochs or sample size while holding model size fixed.
record.test_reason: Besides its monotonization method, the paper derives (Prop. 3.14, 3.15, S.3.1–S.3.3) and simulates (Figs. 3–4) the baseline risk of min-ℓ2 and min-ℓ1 norm least squares across p/n. Both diverge at the interpolation threshold and fall again past it. This bears on V4 in linear regression. Because the asymptotic profile depends only on p/n, it also bears on V3 in theory. Fig. 8 adds an optimally tuned lasso curve bearing on V6's regularization clause. No deep-network, epoch, or effective-complexity analysis is done.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose cross-validation-based zero-step (bagging-like) and one-step (boosting-like) procedures. They prove these asymptotically monotonize risk in the aspect ratio under mild assumptions, and illustrate this with MN2LS and MN1LS, whose base risks diverge at γ=1. Correction: the statement that optimally tuned ridge need not be monotone is attributed to Hastie et al. (2019), not shown in their own Fig. 8. Their own finding is that zero- and one-step risks approach optimal ridge or lasso risk, and that optimally tuned lasso is monotone in their sparse example.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes cross-validation-based risk profiles and mitigation for linear predictors, rather than the original deep-network size, epoch, and data sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The simulations vary SNR and use dense MN2LS versus sparse MN1LS settings; the regularization comparison differs between ridge and lasso.
record.problems: The numerical curves are reported in figures without extracted point values or uncertainty intervals. The theoretical profiles rely on stated distributional and asymptotic assumptions. The experiments vary feature dimension at fixed sample size and do not test epochs or increasing sample size at fixed model size.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results were omitted. Results for the proposed zero-step and one-step procedures were left out because they measure modified procedures rather than the base double-descent behavior; cited results from other work were also excluded.

untested.parts: No deep networks; no model-size sweep of neural networks.
Simulations vary p at fixed n. There is no empirical sample-size sweep, and the V3 evidence is theoretical (proportional asymptotics).
Only linear least-squares interpolators (MN2LS, MN1LS). No other model classes and no classical U-shaped regime are examined.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Noise as the driver of the peak (noise is always present), splitting into multiple peaks (cited from Li & Wei, not shown), and optimal ridge, which appears only in a figure with no stated result.
No re-expression of capacity as an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Closed-form isotropic MN2LS overparameterized risk ρ²(1−1/φ)+σ²/(φ−1)+σ². For SNR>1 it has an interior minimum at φ=√s/(√s−1); for SNR≤1 it decreases monotonically to s. This locates the second descent and how it depends on SNR.
Asymptotic MN2LS and MN1LS profiles (MN1LS at sparsity 0.01), described as diverging around the interpolation threshold of 1.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'challenges' label is removed: it rested on a cited result. Even if it held, non-monotone risk is not the same as a peak persisting. Bagging (M>1) lowering risk near the threshold is a property of the authors' own method, not a base-procedure result. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweep and peak near the training-set interpolation size.
A sweep that increases training sample count near the interpolation threshold.
The study considers MN2LS and MN1LS, not a broad survey of model classes.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The reported regularization comparisons do not test whether noise drives peaks or whether peaks split into multiple descents.
Re-expressing the second descent against an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: MN2LS (minimum ℓ2-norm least squares) predictor
rows.size_stated: p features; proportional asymptotics with p/m → φ
rows.operation_detail: Derived the asymptotic squared prediction-risk profile across feature-to-sample ratios.

conditions.value: Theorem 3 setting of Hastie et al. (2019), as specified in Supplement S.3.1
φ=p/m; profile includes φ<1, φ=1, φ>1, and φ→∞

rows.value: Rdet(φ)=σ²/(1−φ) for φ∈(0,1); Rdet(1)=∞; for φ∈(1,∞) the profile is given by (E.45); as φ→∞ it tends to ρ²∫r dG(r)+σ². The text describes the profile as non-monotone and says it diverges around the interpolation threshold.
rows.note: The paper derives and extends the profile under stated assumptions; it does not test a deep network.
rows.check: Add V3. The profile Rdet(φ) depends only on φ=p/m, and the paper notes that increasing φ equals decreasing sample size. Its own text says this implies more samples can worsen risk near φ=1. The bias and variance formulas extend Hastie et al. (2019), conditioned on (X,Y), and add the φ→∞ limit, so part of this is a re-derivation of a cited result.

rows.subject: optimally regularized ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Compared the risk curve for optimally tuned ridge regression across aspect ratios.
rows.value: figure only; the text states that optimally tuned ridge need not have monotone risk
rows.note: This result runs against the version's claim that the peak disappears under optimally tuned regularization.
rows.check: The claim that optimally tuned ridge 'need not have monotone risk' is a cited result ('see, for example, Figure 1 of Hastie et al. (2019)'). It is not stated for the paper's own Fig. 8 left panel. That text only says zero- and one-step risk is close to optimal ridge in a well-specified dense model. The row should not be 'reversed' and cannot support a V6 challenge.

relationships.condition: MN2LS (dense) and MN1LS (sparse) linear regression, isotropic Gaussian features, SNR 1 and 4
relationships.reason: Derived profiles and simulations show risk diverging at p/n=1 and decreasing again past it (r1–r5).
relationships.display_finding: Derived risk profiles and simulations diverged at p/n=1 and declined beyond it for SNR 1 and 4.

relationships.condition: MN2LS and MN1LS under proportional asymptotics (theory only)
relationships.reason: Rdet depends only on p/n and diverges as p/n→1 from above, so adding samples at fixed p near the threshold raises risk (r1).
relationships.display_finding: The deterministic risk depended only on p/n and diverged as p/n approached 1 from above.

relationships.condition: Optimally tuned lasso, sparse linear model, n=100, SNR=4
relationships.reason: The text states risk is monotone for optimally tuned lasso, so no peak under optimal regularization in this setting (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Optimally tuned lasso produced monotone risk without a peak in the sparse linear simulation.
